units.text: Routing strategy: partner with RouteSprout now, and buy only on conditional terms. Do not buy RouteSprout on the proposed terms in 2027. Partner now, and keep a conditional option to buy later at no more than $8.5M upfront. (Revised answer: partner now to meet the customer need within the cash limits; turn the acquisition into an option exercised only if diligence and partnership data clear defined thresholds.)
units.source_loc: Slide 1 title; Slide 2 title; Slide 3 revised answer

units.text: Question for the board (March 2027 meeting): Should Atlas buy RouteSprout in 2027, and on what terms, rather than build or partner?
All figures are from the briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data) or are labelled team assumptions. $ in millions unless stated.
Reject / decline the $18.0M all-cash deal (Path A) and the staged deal as structured (Path B). (Also decision 1 requested in March 2027.)
Sign a two-year RouteSprout routing partnership ($1.2M minimum, live summer 2027) that includes a right of first refusal and a pre-agreed conditional purchase option.
Exercise the purchase option at a Q1 2028 gate only if six evidence thresholds are met.
Neither acquisition path stays inside the cash limits: neither keeps cash above the $9.0M board floor once 18 months of operating losses are counted.

Path A needs $22.0M ($18.0M + $4.0M) against a $15.0M ceiling on initial spend ($24.0M − $9.0M). It leaves $2.0M before any operating losses; the $15.0M limit rules it out on its own. Path A is worse at every step.

Path B fits at signing ($14.5M = $11.0M upfront + $3.5M integration; cash at close 9.5 = floor + 0.5, i.e. $0.5M headroom), but 18 months of operating drag takes cash to $7.2–8.2M by end-2028, below the $9.0M floor.
Nothing in the plan funds the $7.0M earnout due in 2029 (the earnout has no funding source).
The value case is overstated, and payback takes more than 15 years.

On recognised ARR the $18.0M price is 3.75x revenue ($18.0M ÷ $4.8M ARR, Atlas finance), not the sellers' 2.5x of bookings ($18.0M ÷ $7.2M bookings) — 50% higher than the sellers' 2.5x. Atlas policy (corporate finance) is to value recurring revenue on recognised ARR.

The $2.4M cross-sell is ARR, not EBITDA. After margin, support and RouteSprout's losses it adds about $0.1M a year (+0.07), and loses $1.2M a year (−1.21) in the low case. Sellers' pitch counts the full $2.4M as EBITDA (chart: 2.4 vs 0.07 vs −1.21).
Customer and execution risk is high and not priced in.
Annual customer logo churn rose from 12% (FY2024) to 21% (FY2026); sellers' case shows 0%. RouteSprout's customers are churning faster.

Revenue is concentrated: 58% of ARR sits in 41 accounts. FY2026 ARR by group: 41 large accounts $2.78M; 269 other accounts $2.02M (58% vs 42% of $4.8M ARR) — about $68K per large account against about $7.5K per other account.
The sellers' case assumes 100% renewal of all 310 accounts, which is 0% churn (every account renews).
30% of the integration work is unscoped, and the six-month plan assumes zero change-management delay.
The synergy, retention and integration claims rest on correlations and untested plans, not on evidence of cause (the synergy evidence is correlation only).
Against the board's four criteria, only the partnership passes (all four) in 2027. The build is the fallback, not the first move.
Partnership: at most $1.2M is at risk, it is live this summer (summer 2027), and no customers have to migrate.
The partnership earns more than ownership at any routing ARR below about $3.5M ($3.47M), well above the Sales VP's unsigned $2.4M base case.
Building is affordable but cannot ship before late 2028, so it misses the renewal cycles the partnership can serve from summer 2027.
Buying stays possible, but only on conditional terms: at most $8.5M upfront (about 1.8x verified ARR), priced on QoE-verified recognised ARR excluding pilots; reduce by about 1.8x any ARR shortfall.

units.text: Earnout: up to $9.5M more if earned, so the total stays within the sellers' $18.0M headline.
units.correct_version: The $8.5M upfront + $9.5M earnout keeps total consideration at $18.0M — the same figure the deck argues is overstated (3.75x recognised ARR). A consistent version either lowers the total or explains explicitly why $18.0M is acceptable when the second $9.5M is paid only on earned results.
units.source_loc: Slide 2; Slide 15 title and earnout row; Slide 17 decision 4

units.text: Payment protection: pay the earnout only while cash stays above $9.0M plus a buffer (no payment that takes cash below the floor). Defer any excess, or settle it in Atlas equity if shareholders approve.

Integrate through the API first (API plus single sign-on first), and keep RouteSprout's interface until its large accounts renew: no interface replacement or record migration before large-account renewals. Fully scoped budget of no more than $4.0M, including support.
Initial hypothesis: Atlas should buy RouteSprout in 2027, using the staged structure (Path B, $11.0M upfront) to fit the $15.0M cash ceiling, because it is the fastest way to own routing.
The starting hypothesis fails four of the five tests it has to pass, and the fifth is unproven (verdicts as listed: Fail, Fail, Fail, Unproven, Fail).

Test 1 — Affordable: cash stays at or above the $9.0M floor through 2028, and the earnout can be funded. Evidence: Path B leaves $0.5M headroom at signing and falls to $7.2–8.2M by end-2028; the $7.0M earnout has no funding source.

Test 2 — Fairly priced: the price rests on verified recurring revenue. Evidence: 3.75x recognised ARR, not 2.5x; bookings include multi-year contract value and pilots; no quality-of-earnings (QoE) review has been done.

Test 3 — Pays back: positive incremental contribution within a reasonable horizon. Evidence: run-rate contribution is +$0.07M (base) or −$1.21M (low) while integration support runs; payback takes more than 15 years.

Test 4 — Protects customers: RouteSprout and Atlas renewals and 99.7% uptime survive integration. Evidence: churn rose from 12% to 21%; the case assumes 100% renewal; replacing the interface before renewals risks churn; no cohort data exists.

Test 5 — Beats the alternatives on cash, payback, continuity and execution. Evidence: the partnership earns more below about $3.5M of routing ARR and risks at most $1.2M; building is slower but cheaper.

Lowest cash balance through end-2028 compared with the $9.0M floor, $M (0 = at the floor; below 0 = breach). Base case (cross-sell $2.4M): D Internal build 11.6; C Partnership 13.8; B Staged acquisition −0.8; A Full cash acquisition −8.3. Low case (cross-sell $0.8M): D 11.6; C 13.8; B −1.8; A −9.3.

How Path B falls below the floor (Jul 2027 – Dec 2028), $M: unrestricted cash today 24.0; upfront price −11.0; integration (Path B estimate) −3.5; cash at close 9.5; RouteSprout EBITDA (−1.0/yr × 1.5) −1.5; integration-era support (−0.85/yr × 1.5) −1.3; cross-sell gross profit (linear ramp, 80%) +1.4 base / +0.5 low; lowest cash end-2028 8.2 base / 7.2 low; headroom vs $9.0M floor −0.8 base / −1.8 low.
Operating drag over 18 months: −1.0×1.5 − 0.85×1.5 + (ARR/2)×1.5×0.8 → −$1.3M (base ARR 2.4) / −$2.3M (low ARR 0.8). This alone breaches the $9.0M floor.

Cash chart assumptions: C assumes zero partner revenue (worst case). D assumes the full $3.4M is spent before launch. A and B include RouteSprout losses and integration-era support from a July 2027 close.
Path B's $0.5M margin is also exposed to three cash calls the deal case does not price: unscoped integration work, the integration cap and the $7.0M earnout.
Unscoped integration work: every $1 of overrun is $1 below the floor. Path B's $3.5M estimate leaves $0.5M under the $4.0M cap.

The $4.0M integration cap explicitly covers "systems migration and customer support"; the pack calls the $0.85M/yr integration-era support "another" cost, so it may count. If it counts: A = $4.0M + $1.3M = $5.3M and B = $3.5M + $1.3M = $4.8M; both breach the cap. If it does not, it hits cash instead.

The $7.0M earnout due in 2029 is payable after 2028 if growth and renewal tests pass; the CFO notes an earnout "does not eliminate future cash strain". Cash is already below the floor at end-2028. Base-case run-rate contribution of $0.92M/yr would need about 7.6 years to fund it (7.0 ÷ 0.92).

Uptime service credits: large customers need 99.7% uptime. A missed quarter triggers service credits and renewal risk that the sellers leave out. Not quantified in the pack. The risk only runs one way, and a full record migration makes it larger.
So what: the problem is not just the headline price. Any acquisition must leave room for 18 months of losses, a contingency on unscoped work, and an earnout that does not have to be paid in cash.
Path B upfront only: $11.0M ÷ $4.8M ARR = 2.29x (2.3x).

Why $7.2M of bookings is the wrong denominator: it is not recurring revenue. The audit notes say the $7.2M includes multi-year contract value and one-time pilots; it is not a current recurring revenue rate. It is unsuitable for valuation or for projecting retention.
Pilots are counted as if they renew. The sellers make no adjustment for one-year pilots that will not renew, so bookings overstate both value and retention-adjusted revenue.
Even the $4.8M ARR figure is unverified: there is no QoE review and no independently verified ARR schedule. The 42% growth figure stops before the last quarter.
There are no earnings to support the price. EBITDA is −$1.0M, including founder salaries, so the price relies entirely on revenue quality and on synergies.
Path B's total, including the full earnout, is also $18.0M, which is 3.75x ARR. The structure moves when the money is paid, not how much is paid (staging lowers upfront cash, not the total).

Bridge from cross-sell ARR to contribution, $M per year (base / low): cross-sell ARR by end-2028 2.40 / 0.80 (Sales VP / finance); × 80% incremental gross margin 1.92 / 0.64; − integration-era support −0.85 / −0.85; = cross-sell contribution 1.07 / −0.21; + RouteSprout standalone EBITDA −1.00 / −1.00 (FY2026, held flat); = contribution in integration era 0.07 / −1.21.
Memo: contribution after integration support ends 0.92 (base) / −0.36 (low) — an assumption (0.8 × ARR − 1.0).

Still optimistic: the contribution bridge ignores the sellers' assumption of 100% renewal. At 21% logo churn, about $1.0M of RouteSprout's $4.8M ARR is at risk each year (21% × $4.8M ≈ $1.0M/yr; logo churn used as a proxy for revenue churn; not in the base numbers).
No cost savings and no retention uplift are assumed, as the pack instructs (the routing-retention link is confounded), and the low case is the one finance considers plausible if churn persists.
RouteSprout EBITDA held at −$1.0M/yr (FY2026, held flat): 42% growth and 21% churn pull in opposite directions. Breakeven would lower the cross-sell needed to about $1.06M.
Buying takes more than 15 years to pay back, and never does in the low case. Building takes about 5 years, and partnering risks at most $1.2M.

A · Full cash acquisition: cash committed $22.0M; annual run-rate contribution +0.92 base / −0.36 low (+0.07 / −1.21 during integration); simple payback ≈24 years / never (22.0 ÷ 0.92). RouteSprout's losses absorb most of the cross-sell gross profit.

B · Staged acquisition: cash committed $14.5M upfront + $7.0M earnout; contribution +0.92 / −0.36 (same business); simple payback ≈16 years (23 with earnout) / never. The earnout is paid only in the base case.

C · Partnership: cash committed $1.2M (two-year minimum); contribution +0.46 base / −0.25 low (after the $0.6M/yr minimum; 0.8 × 0.55 × ARR − 0.6); simple payback ≈1.1 years / not within the 2-year term. Breaks even at $1.36M of routing ARR (0.6 ÷ 0.44). The worst-case loss is $1.2M; in the low case it is about $0.5M over two years.

D · Internal build: $3.4M through 2028 + $0.4M/yr operations after launch; contribution +0.64 from 2029 if $1.3M ARR arrives (1.3 × 80% − 0.4 = 0.64; low case not given); payback ≈5.3 years after launch (3.4 ÷ 0.64). Assumes an on-time launch.

How to read payback: payback = cash committed ÷ annual contribution after that path's running costs (simple, undiscounted). It is deliberately simple; the board asked us not to build a precise DCF from inputs we do not have.

Partner economics: for C, cross-sell ARR uses the same $0.8–2.4M range at 80% gross margin and Atlas's 55% share; the $1.2M minimum is a fixed cost that cannot be recouped. Conservative — crediting the minimum would improve the partnership case. Because the partner offering is limited, the low end is more likely.
Concentration magnifies the risk: losing a handful of the 41 large accounts would wipe out a year of cross-sell.
People drive renewals, not features: customer success interviews found account managers drive renewal decisions, so RouteSprout's account managers matter as much as its code.
Interface timing matters: the product VP warns that replacing RouteSprout's interface before large customers renew could add churn.
No cohort data: we cannot yet tell whether churn sits in small or large accounts. That is the first diligence item.

Deal-case claim "Customers who use routing renew at 95%, so routing causes retention": routing users are mostly larger, multi-branch firms with dedicated customer success teams; smaller non-users renew at 78%; the feature effect is not isolated. Treatment: we credit no retention uplift to Atlas's core base, and we keep RouteSprout's account managers.

Deal-case claim "Integration works when the product is under one general manager": the cited companies were on average twice as large, with lower churn; the link between integration spend and cross-sell is a correlation with no causal identification. Treatment: not transferable. We do not underwrite the $2.4M cross-sell. Earnouts carry that risk instead.

Deal-case claim "Six months and $4.0M to integrate": 30% of the work is unscoped and the plan assumes zero change-management delay; API plus single sign-on (SSO) is simpler than migrating records and support. Treatment: integrate through the API first; scope 100% of the work and price the contingency before signing.
Treatment of "2.5x recurring revenue" and $7.2M of "annual recurring new sales": value on QoE-verified recognised ARR only.

Key people stay (implicit claim): a substantial part of the value depends on keeping key engineers for at least two years; no agreements are in place. Signed 24-month retention agreements (key engineers and account managers, signed before close) become a condition of the deal.

Criterion: Cash vs $9.0M floor — A Fail ($22.0M out; cash is at $2.0M before losses); B Fail ($14.5M at signing, then $7.2–8.2M by end-2028); C Pass (at most $1.2M; cash stays at $22.8M or more); D Pass ($3.4M; cash stays at $20.6M or more).

Criterion: Payback — A Fail (about 24 years in the base case, never in the low case); B Fail (about 16 years, 23 with the earnout, never in the low case); C Watch (breaks even at $1.36M of routing ARR; loss capped at $1.2M); D Watch (about 5.3 years after a late-2028 launch).

Criterion: Customer continuity — A Fail (full migration before renewals, with churn at 21%); B Watch (same migration risk; the earnout ties sellers to renewals); C Pass (no migration; prospects are served from summer 2027); D Watch (nothing to offer prospects until late 2028).

Criterion: Execution capacity — A Fail (30% unscoped, zero-delay plan, key engineers at risk); B Fail (same integration load on a thinner budget); C Watch (depends on the partner's viability; roadmap has to be shared); D Fail (at least 18 months; displaces the compliance upgrade).

Strategic fit (tie-break) — A Pass (owns routing and RouteSprout's team); B Pass (owns routing once integrated); C Watch (no ownership, but first refusal keeps the option); D Pass (Atlas owns the IP, but it arrives late).
Ratings legend: Pass = meets the board limit with margin; Watch = meets it with a risk to manage; Fail = breaches a hard limit or has no credible path. Only one routing strategy can run in 2027.

Contribution formulas (before acquisition capital): Acquire, integration era: 0.8 × ARR − 1.85 (less $1.0M losses and $0.85M support). Partner: 0.44 × ARR − 0.6 (55% of gross profit, less $0.6M/yr minimum). Acquisition after integration support ends: 0.8 × ARR − 1.0.
Partner vs acquire by routing ARR: $0.8M (low): partner −0.25, acquire −1.21 → Partner better. $2.4M (base): partner +0.46, acquire +0.07 → Partner better. $3.47M: +0.93 vs +0.93 → Equal.
Ownership wins only at scale: 0.36 × ARR = 1.25 gives $3.47M (0.44x − 0.6 = 0.8x − 1.85). Once support ends and the partner minimum lapses, the crossover is still $2.78M (0.8x − 1.0 = 0.44x).
Capital is excluded: the crossover chart ignores the $14.5–22.0M paid to acquire. Including it widens the partnership's lead.
The build ARR timing is doubtful: the pack calls it "2028 ARR", but a late-2028 launch makes that unlikely. We treat it as a 2029 run-rate.
Hidden cost of building: it displaces a planned compliance upgrade. The customer cost of that delay has not been estimated.
Role of the internal build: the fallback if the partnership underperforms and the buy terms fail at the 2028 gate.

Timeline (Q1 2027 – Q2 2029): C · Partnership — contract, live summer 2027, two-year term to mid-2029. A/B · Acquisition — diligence, integrate (6 mo plan), delay risk. D · Internal build — build ≥ 18 months, launch, ramp to $1.3M ARR. Markers: Board, Mar 2027; Gate, Q1 2028.

Timing assumptions: acquisition closes July 2027 after the March board and a roughly 3-month diligence, so 18 months to end-2028 (a later close shifts the timing but not the conclusion). The build starts after the March 2027 board and takes at least 18 months, so launch comes no earlier than Q4 2028. Atlas can run only one major routing strategy in 2027.
Sign the partnership on terms that cap cost, protect uptime and stop a competitor from capturing RouteSprout.
Scope and price (as offered): non-exclusive routing API with a $1.2M two-year minimum. Gross profit splits 55% to Atlas and 45% to RouteSprout.
Ask: credit the minimum — count minimum payments against RouteSprout's 45% share. This cuts the $1.36M break-even and the $1.2M maximum loss.
Service level: at least 99.7% quarterly uptime, with service credits passed back to Atlas to match the credits Atlas owes its large customers.
Segment exclusivity (ask): exclusivity in utilities and repair contractors, Atlas's core segments. Negotiate for it, but do not make it a condition.
Change of control: right of first refusal on any sale of RouteSprout, plus a right to terminate if a competitor buys it. The founders want to sell, so this is the key protection.
Pre-agreed purchase option: attach the conditional term sheet (p.15), exercisable at the Q1 2028 gate. Partnership fees paid are credited against the price.
Information rights: customer-level churn cohorts, the ARR schedule and pipeline data. These double as diligence evidence.
Continuity and roadmap: source-code escrow and data portability in case RouteSprout fails (EBITDA −$1.0M). Share only interface-level roadmap, through a clean team.
Partnership walk-away: if RouteSprout refuses first-refusal or change-of-control protection, the roadmap risk outweighs the speed benefit. Reopen the build decision.
Earnout measures, measured over 2028–29: top-41 ARR retained, logo churn at or below 12%, signed cross-sell ARR in bands from $1.4M to $2.4M, and 99.7% uptime.
Acquisition walk-away: if the sellers demand more than $8.5M upfront or all cash, keep the partnership and do not buy.

Deriving the upfront ceiling, $M: cash above the $9.0M floor 15.0; − integration at the $4.0M cap (30% unscoped, so assume it is all used) −4.0; − 18-month operating drag, low case (losses + support − cross-sell gross profit) −2.3; = maximum affordable upfront 8.7; recommended ceiling (≈1.8x $4.8M ARR) 8.5.
The upfront ceiling drops $1-for-$1 for any partnership fees not credited at close, and for any audited integration budget above the cap.
The $0.2M buffer (8.7 vs 8.5) is thin. If diligence shows churn concentrated in large accounts, do not raise the upfront to compensate.
Six pieces of missing information would change the recommendation, and each has a threshold set in advance.

Threshold 1 — QoE-verified ARR. Today: $4.8M, unverified; bookings include pilots. Threshold to proceed with buying: recognised ARR of at least $4.8M, excluding pilots. If not met: cut the price about 1.8x per $1 of shortfall, or walk away.

Threshold 2 — Customer-level churn cohort. Today: 21% logo churn, no cohort data. Threshold: churn falling toward 12% (FY2024), and stable top-41 accounts. If not met: stay with the partnership; do not buy.

Threshold 3 — Signed routing demand. Today: $0 signed; $2.4M is the Sales VP's view. Threshold: at least $1.36M run-rate shows demand; about $2.3M is needed to cover RouteSprout's losses. If not met: below $1.36M, reconsider routing altogether, including the build.
units.correct_version: A $1.36M run-rate is only the partnership's break-even; it lets the buy gate clear well below the deck's own crossover, where the partnership still out-earns ownership ($3.47M of routing ARR in the integration era, $2.78M after support ends; about $2.3M merely covers RouteSprout's losses). A consistent buy threshold requires routing ARR at or credibly heading above the crossover, or an explicit reason why exercising the option below it is still right. Below $1.36M, reconsider routing altogether, including the build.

units.text: Threshold 4 — RouteSprout standalone EBITDA. Today: −$1.0M a year. Threshold: at breakeven, ownership needs only about $1.06M of cross-sell (0.85 ÷ 0.8). If not met: keep the earnout weighted to results.
Threshold 5 — Audited integration budget. Today: 30% unscoped, zero-delay plan. Threshold: fully scoped at no more than $4.0M, including support and contingency. If not met: do not buy.

Threshold 6 — Key people and seller terms. Today: no retention agreements; $18.0M all cash. Threshold: 24-month agreements signed, and sellers accept at most $8.5M upfront. If not met: keep the partnership; revisit the build in 2028.
Early trigger (any time): if a competing buyer / bid emerges, use the right of first refusal on the pre-agreed terms, but only if items 1, 2 and 5 have already cleared.
In March 2027 the board should approve the partnership, fund diligence and set the walk-away terms. The decision to buy follows at a Q1 2028 gate.
Decision 2: Approve the two-year RouteSprout partnership (at most $1.2M minimum) with the protections on p.14.
Decision 3: Approve preliminary diligence: QoE, customer cohorts, integration scoping and key-person review. The CFO will size the budget, which the pack does not give.
Decision 4: Mandate negotiation of the conditional term sheet: at most $8.5M upfront and up to $9.5M earned, with a set walk-away.
Decision 5: Defer the internal build, and revisit it at the gate if the partnership underperforms.
Apr–Jun 2027: Sign the partnership. Run diligence in parallel and negotiate the conditional term sheet.
Summer 2027: Routing goes live with the enterprise prospects that asked for it. Start tracking attach and ARR.
Q3–Q4 2027: QoE and cohort results arrive. Watch the RouteSprout renewal outcomes for its 41 large accounts.
Q1 2028 gate: Buy if all six thresholds are met (p.16). Otherwise continue the partnership, or start the build if demand is proven but the partner falls short.
units.correct_version: As written, the six thresholds can all be met with routing ARR (from $1.36M) well below the deck's own crossover ($3.47M, or $2.78M after support ends), where its analysis says the partnership earns more than ownership. A consistent gate: buy only if all six thresholds are met AND routing ARR evidence shows ownership beats the partnership (at or credibly above the crossover), or the deck states explicitly why exercising the option below the crossover is still right. Otherwise continue the partnership, or start the build if demand is proven but the partner falls short.

units.text: Interpretation: partnering with RouteSprout in 2027 and buying it in 2028 counts as one routing strategy (the same product), so the plan respects the one-strategy rule. If the board disagrees, the 2028 gate becomes a choice between partnership and build only.
The recommendation carries five main risks. Each has a mitigation, and the cash downside is capped at $1.2M.

Risk: RouteSprout is sold to a competitor during the partnership. Why: the founders want to sell; Atlas will have shared roadmap details. Mitigation: right of first refusal, termination on change of control, interface-only roadmap through a clean team. Residual: Medium — Atlas would lose its routing supplier, and the build becomes the fallback.

Risk: The partner offering is too limited for enterprise prospects. Why: the partner offer is "limited"; prospects may want deep integration. Mitigation: pilot with the requesting prospects in summer 2027; measure attach before the gate. Residual: Medium — prospects may wait for the 2028 decision.

Risk: Routing ARR stays below the $1.36M break-even. Why: the $1.2M minimum is a fixed cost. Mitigation: ask for the minimum to be credited against the 45% share; weight the gate to signed ARR. Residual: Low — at most $1.2M; about $0.5M net in the low case.

Risk: RouteSprout fails financially. Why: EBITDA is −$1.0M and churn is 21%; its cash position is unknown. Mitigation: source-code escrow, data portability and uptime service credits; our minimum also funds the partner. Residual: Medium — service disruption, so we need an SLA tied to 99.7%.

Risk: The sellers reject the conditional terms. Why: the founders asked for $18.0M in cash. Mitigation: walk away; the partnership meets the customer need without ownership. Residual: Low — we give up the option of owning routing, not the capability.
Appendix: the analysis separates pack evidence from team assumptions, and each assumption is conservative or is tested on the slide that uses it.
Cross-sell ramp: linear from 0 to target by end-2028; average ARR over the period is half the target.
Integration-era support (evidence + assumption): $0.85M/yr for 18 months, then ends. Amount from the pack; duration assumed. Shown as cost to cash or to the $4.0M cap (p.5).
Atlas core operations (evidence): about cash-break-even; no offset from, or drain on, core cash.

Appendix: every figure in the deck can be traced to pack inputs through simple arithmetic (calculations table: initial cash ceiling $24.0M − $9.0M = $15.0M; Path A / B cash out at close $22.0M / $14.5M; valuation multiples 2.5x / 3.75x / 2.3x; partnership break-even $1.36M; crossover $3.47M ARR; build $0.64M/yr and ≈5.3 years; earnout funding ≈7.6 years; upfront ceiling $8.7M → $8.5M; concentration ≈$68K / ≈$7.5K per account).
